set1.q: How does chronic mitral regurgitation progress?
opts: Annular dilation, tricuspid leak, then isolated right failure
Annular dilation causing tricuspid regurgitation is a right-sided process. Chronic mitral regurgitation ends in combined right and left heart failure after pulmonary hypertension.
Left heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, then both sides fail

Correct. Chronic mitral regurgitation dilates the left ventricle with eccentric hypertrophy, causing left heart failure, then pulmonary hypertension, and finally combined right and left heart failure.
Left atrial clot, stroke, then sudden cardiac death
Clot and stroke are mitral stenosis worries through atrial fibrillation. Chronic mitral regurgitation runs from left heart failure to pulmonary hypertension to combined failure.
Concentric hypertrophy, stiffness, then preserved-fraction failure
Concentric hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction is the pressure-overload course of aortic stenosis. Mitral regurgitation volume-loads and dilates the ventricle.

set1.q: When should pulmonic stenosis be referred to cardiology?
opts: Only if it is part of tetralogy of Fallot
Congenital or not, pulmonic stenosis present on an echocardiogram is referred to a cardiologist.
Only after a 20-year follow-up
The 94% 20-year survival describes mild to moderate disease; it does not delay referral. Echocardiographic pulmonic stenosis is referred.
Whenever it is seen on echocardiogram
Correct. Whether congenital or related to heart failure, pulmonic stenosis should be referred to a cardiologist whenever it is present on an echocardiogram.
Only once right heart failure appears
Referral does not wait for heart failure. Pulmonic stenosis seen on an echocardiogram is referred to cardiology.

set1.q: How is pulmonic regurgitation usually discovered?
opts: Incidentally, on echo or examination
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or on physical examination; management is to treat the underlying condition.
By catheterization after syncope
Catheterization after syncope is not how pulmonic regurgitation comes to light. It is usually found incidentally on an echocardiogram or examination.
By an electrocardiogram showing right axis deviation
Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy is the pulmonic stenosis electrocardiogram. Regurgitation is usually found incidentally on echo or examination.
By a chest radiograph after hemoptysis
Hemoptysis belongs to mitral stenosis. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or physical examination.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: What should a patient receiving a mechanical heart valve be told about anticoagulation?
opts: It is only for surgery
Heparin bridging covers surgery, but the underlying need is lifelong. A mechanical valve needs a vitamin K antagonist for life.
It will be needed for life
Correct. A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist, most commonly warfarin, monitored against an international normalized ratio target.
It stops after six weeks
Short postoperative anticoagulation describes a bioprosthetic valve. A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation.
Aspirin alone will do
Antiplatelet agents are ranked below vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves. Lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy is required.

set1.q: How long after rheumatic fever is rheumatic mitral stenosis usually diagnosed?
opts: About 5 years
Five years is too soon. The valve thickens and narrows slowly, and diagnosis usually comes about 20 years after the rheumatic fever.
About 50 years
Fifty years overshoots it. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is usually diagnosed about 20 years after the episode of rheumatic fever.
About 20 years
Correct. Mitral stenosis from rheumatic fever is usually diagnosed about 20 years after the fever, and symptoms stay rare until the orifice has narrowed to about a third of normal.
Within 1 year
The narrowing develops slowly over decades. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is usually diagnosed about 20 years after the rheumatic fever, not within the first year.

set1.q: Rheumatic heart disease is an autoimmune reaction to which infection?
opts: Viridans group streptococcus
Viridans streptococci are not what drives rheumatic heart disease. The autoimmune reaction follows group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection.
Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus
Correct. Rheumatic heart disease is an autoimmune reaction to group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. It is an acquired cause of aortic stenosis and the most common cause of mitral stenosis.
Group B beta-hemolytic streptococcus
Group B streptococcus is not the trigger. Rheumatic heart disease follows group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection as an autoimmune reaction.
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia
Staphylococcal bloodstream infection causes infective endocarditis, a separate acquired valve disease. Rheumatic heart disease is autoimmune, after group A streptococcal infection.

set1.q: What therapy does asymptomatic mitral stenosis in sinus rhythm need?
opts: A loop diuretic
Loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide are for symptoms of dyspnea and orthopnea. Without symptoms, in sinus rhythm, no therapy is needed.
Balloon valvotomy
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy is for severe mitral stenosis with symptomatic dyspnea or pulmonary hypertension, not for asymptomatic patients.
Valve replacement
Valve replacement is reserved for moderate symptoms or pulmonary hypertension in severe disease. Asymptomatic mitral stenosis in sinus rhythm needs no therapy.
No therapy
Correct. Asymptomatic mitral stenosis with sinus rhythm needs no therapy. Loop diuretics are added once dyspnea and orthopnea appear, and intervention waits for severe disease with symptoms.

set1.q: Which study diagnoses tricuspid regurgitation?
opts: Doppler echocardiogram

Correct. Doppler echocardiography shows the regurgitation and the leaflets, which may be prolapsed, scarred or displaced. Referral follows when it is identified on echo or with right heart failure symptoms.
Left heart catheterization
Left heart catheterization is the definitive study for aortic stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation is diagnosed on Doppler echocardiography.
Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph cannot show regurgitant flow across the tricuspid valve. Doppler echocardiography diagnoses it.
Electrocardiogram
The electrocardiogram cannot show a leaking valve. Tricuspid regurgitation is diagnosed with Doppler echocardiography.

set1.q: Which echocardiogram finding diagnoses mitral valve prolapse?
opts: Thickened, redundant leaflets over 5 mm
Correct. The echocardiogram shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets over 5 mm that flare into the left atrium during systole. Echocardiography is the diagnostic test.
Thickened, immobile leaflets, narrow orifice
Thickened, immobile leaflets with a narrowed orifice are the rheumatic mitral stenosis picture. Prolapse shows redundant leaflets over 5 mm.
Calcified aortic leaflets, poor opening
Calcified aortic leaflets with reduced systolic opening are aortic stenosis. Mitral valve prolapse shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
A dilated aortic root over 4 cm
A dilated aortic root is a cause of aortic regurgitation. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by redundant mitral leaflets over 5 mm.

set1.q: What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients older than 70?
opts: Infective endocarditis
Endocarditis is an acquired cause and involves the aortic valve in about 20% of cases, but the leading cause over 70 is degenerative disease.
Degenerative (atherosclerotic) disease
Correct. Degenerative heart disease, the atherosclerotic process driven by hyperlipidemia, diabetes and smoking, is the most common cause of aortic stenosis over 70.
A congenital bicuspid aortic valve
A bicuspid aortic valve is the most common cause under 70. Over 70 the leading cause is degenerative, atherosclerotic disease.
Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic heart disease is an acquired cause of aortic stenosis, but not the leading one at any age. Over 70 it is degenerative disease.

set1.q: Which neck findings fit tricuspid regurgitation?
opts: A collapsing pulse with head bobbing
A collapsing pulse with head bobbing (Corrigan and de Musset signs) belongs to aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation shows venous findings in the neck.
Hoarseness from nerve compression
Hoarseness from the left atrium pressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is mitral stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation shows raised jugular pressure and a thrill.
Raised jugular pressure and a venous thrill
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations and a venous thrill over the right jugular vein, as blood is driven back into the right atrium.
A weak, delayed carotid pulse
A weak, delayed carotid pulse with a forceful apex beat signals severe aortic stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation shows raised jugular pressure and a venous thrill.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: Which long-term anticoagulant class is recommended for a mechanical heart valve?
opts: A vitamin K antagonist
Correct. For patients with mechanical heart valves, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents for long-term management.
An antiplatelet agent
Antiplatelet agents are specifically ranked below vitamin K antagonist therapy for mechanical valves. The recommended long-term class is a vitamin K antagonist.
Heparin alone
Heparin is the bridge used when surgery interrupts warfarin, not the long-term agent. Mechanical valves are managed with a vitamin K antagonist.
No anticoagulant
Mechanical valves need lifelong anticoagulation; it is biological valves that need none beyond the immediate postoperative period. The class is a vitamin K antagonist.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: Which patient is preferred for a bioprosthetic rather than a mechanical valve?
opts: One with mild, asymptomatic valve disease
Mild, asymptomatic disease is not replaced at all. Bioprosthetic valves are preferred when anticoagulation is contraindicated.
One with a contraindication to anticoagulation
Correct. Bioprosthetic valves are preferred when there is any contraindication to anticoagulation, or when life expectancy is shorter than the expected longevity of the bioprosthetic valve.
One whose life expectancy exceeds the valve's
A bioprosthetic valve is preferred when life expectancy is shorter than the valve's expected longevity. Outliving the valve argues the other way.
One who wants lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy
Lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy is the burden of a mechanical valve. Bioprosthetic valves are preferred when anticoagulation is contraindicated.

set1.q: Which procedure treats severe, symptomatic pulmonic stenosis?
opts: Balloon valvuloplasty
Correct. Severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms is treated with diuretics for right heart failure symptoms and pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty; severe congenital disease may need replacement.
A mitral valve clip
A mitral valve clip reduces a mitral regurgitant leak. The right ventricular outflow obstruction of pulmonic stenosis is opened with balloon valvuloplasty.
Tricuspid annuloplasty
Annuloplasty treats tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation. Severe pulmonic stenosis is opened with pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty.
Afterload reduction
Afterload reduction is medical therapy for chronic aortic regurgitation. Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis needs balloon valvuloplasty.

set1.q: What can mitral valve prolapse progress to?
opts: Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is rheumatic worldwide and congenital in the United States. Mitral valve prolapse may progress to mitral regurgitation.
Mitral regurgitation

Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign and asymptomatic but may develop the symptoms and signs of mitral regurgitation, at which point clip, transcatheter replacement or valve replacement are options.
Mitral stenosis
Stenosis comes from rheumatic scarring that thickens and immobilizes the leaflets. Redundant, prolapsing leaflets leak instead: mitral regurgitation.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is degenerative or bicuspid, and unrelated to prolapse of the mitral leaflets. Prolapse may progress to mitral regurgitation.

set1.q: In the United States, what is tricuspid stenosis almost always?
opts: Congenital
Correct. In the United States tricuspid stenosis is almost always congenital, while worldwide it is most commonly due to rheumatic fever. It is most common in women.
Rheumatic
Rheumatic fever is the leading cause worldwide, and it has become rare in developed countries. In the United States tricuspid stenosis is almost always congenital.
Iatrogenic
Iatrogenic injury is the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation. In the United States tricuspid stenosis is almost always congenital.
Degenerative
Degenerative disease is the leading cause of aortic stenosis over 70. In the United States tricuspid stenosis is almost always congenital.

set1.q: Which patients with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult?
opts: Only severe stenosis
Severity drives the surgical decision, not the referral. All patients with echocardiographic aortic stenosis should see cardiology to set their follow-up.
Only those older than 70
Age sorts the likely cause (bicuspid under 70, degenerative over 70), not the referral. All patients with aortic stenosis on echo get a cardiology consult.
All of them
Correct. Every patient with evidence of aortic stenosis on an echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult, to evaluate the valve and decide how often it is followed.
Only symptomatic patients
Symptoms worsen prognosis sharply, but referral does not wait for them. All patients with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult.

set1.q: Which is the high-pressure cause of pulmonic regurgitation?
opts: Carcinoid disease
Carcinoid disease is listed among the low-pressure causes of pulmonic regurgitation. The high-pressure cause is pulmonary hypertension.
Surgical valvotomy
Surgical valvotomy is the iatrogenic, low-pressure cause and the most common overall. The high-pressure cause is pulmonary hypertension.
A bicuspid valve
A congenital bicuspid valve is a low-pressure cause. Pulmonary hypertension is the high-pressure cause of pulmonic regurgitation.
Pulmonary hypertension

Correct. Pulmonary hypertension is the high-pressure cause of pulmonic regurgitation. The low-pressure causes are a congenital bicuspid valve, carcinoid disease and iatrogenic injury, the most common cause overall.

set1.q: Which echocardiogram values define severe mitral stenosis?
opts: Area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >10 mmHg
Correct. Severe mitral stenosis is a valve area under 1.0 cm² with a mean gradient over 10 mmHg and a peak velocity over 3.0 m/s, with proximal flow always present.
Area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg
A mean gradient over 40 mmHg with an area under 1.0 cm² defines severe aortic stenosis. Severe mitral stenosis has a mean gradient over 10 mmHg.
Area <2.5 cm², mean gradient >25 mmHg
These numbers do not define mitral stenosis severity. Severe mitral stenosis is an area under 1.0 cm² with a mean gradient over 10 mmHg.
Area <3.0 cm², mean gradient >60 mmHg
These numbers do not match any mitral grade. Severe mitral stenosis is an area under 1.0 cm², a mean gradient over 10 mmHg and a peak velocity over 3.0 m/s.

set1.q: Which is an acute cause of mitral regurgitation?
opts: Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse is a chronic cause of mitral regurgitation, from myxomatous degeneration. Papillary muscle rupture after infarction is an acute cause.
Dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy is a chronic cause, stretching the valve apparatus over time. Papillary muscle rupture after infarction is acute.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is a chronic cause of mitral regurgitation. Papillary muscle rupture with acute infarction is an acute cause.
Papillary muscle rupture

Correct. Acute mitral regurgitation follows acute myocardial infarction with papillary muscle rupture, chordae tendineae rupture, infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever, acute left ventricular dilation or prosthetic valve failure.

set1.q: What is the survival of untreated severe aortic regurgitation once the ejection fraction falls?
opts: About 10 to 15 years
Ten to fifteen years is how long chronic aortic regurgitation can stay asymptomatic while the ventricle compensates. Once the ejection fraction falls, untreated survival is 2 to 3 years.
About 5 years
Five years is the average survival after angina appears in aortic stenosis. Untreated severe aortic regurgitation with a falling ejection fraction survives about 2 to 3 years.
About 20 years
Twenty years is far too long. Once the ejection fraction falls in severe aortic regurgitation, untreated survival is about 2 to 3 years.
About 2 to 3 years
Correct. Chronic aortic regurgitation with mildly reduced or reduced ejection fraction, symptomatic or not, is a surgical candidate; untreated, survival is only about 2 to 3 years.

set1.q: How does chronic aortic regurgitation remodel the left ventricle?
opts: Concentric hypertrophy, small cavity
Concentric hypertrophy with a small cavity is the pressure-overload response of aortic stenosis, ending in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
Right ventricular pressure overload
Right ventricular pressure overload follows mitral stenosis through pulmonary hypertension, or pulmonic stenosis. Aortic regurgitation volume-loads the left ventricle.
No change until the valve calcifies
The leak itself drives remodeling long before symptoms: eccentric hypertrophy and dilation, ending in reduced ejection fraction.
Eccentric hypertrophy and dilation
Correct. Blood returns to the left ventricle in diastole, the ventricle compensates with eccentric hypertrophy and dilation, and the endpoint is systolic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

set1.q: Which maneuver makes the mitral regurgitation murmur softer?
opts: Standing

Correct. The mitral regurgitation murmur decreases with standing or the Valsalva maneuver. It increases with squatting and handgrip, which raise resistance to ejection and push more blood back into the left atrium.
Squatting
Squatting increases the mitral regurgitation murmur: resistance to ventricular ejection rises and more blood is driven back into the left atrium.
Handgrip
Handgrip raises peripheral resistance to ejection, augmenting regurgitation into the left atrium, so the mitral regurgitation murmur grows louder.
Expiration
Expiration increases left-sided murmurs, mitral regurgitation included, by pushing blood from the lungs into the left heart.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for valvular heart disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set1.q: Which aortic stenosis procedure is used in children and young adults?
opts: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement
Transcatheter replacement is a surgical option for severe aortic stenosis in adults. The procedure listed for children and young adults is percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty.
Mechanical aortic valve replacement
A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation and is a replacement option for severe disease. For children and young adults the listed procedure is balloon valvuloplasty.
Tricuspid annuloplasty
Annuloplasty repairs tricuspid regurgitation caused by annular dilation. Aortic stenosis in children and young adults is treated with percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty.
Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty

Correct. In children and young adults, aortic stenosis is treated with percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty. Older adults with severe symptomatic disease receive valve replacement, such as transcatheter replacement.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for valvular heart disease
set1.q: Which pairing describes a regurgitant (leaking) valve?
opts: Rumbling murmur and volume overload
Rumbling is a stenosis word, used for mitral and tricuspid stenosis. A regurgitant valve produces a blowing murmur with volume overload.
Blowing murmur and pressure overload
Blowing is right for regurgitation, but the overload is wrong: backflow adds volume. Pressure overload comes from pushing blood through a narrowed, stenotic valve.
Blowing murmur and volume overload
Correct. Regurgitation is abnormal backflow through a valve that does not close completely. The murmur is described as blowing, and the extra blood returning each beat produces volume overload.
Harsh murmur and pressure overload
Harsh with pressure overload is the stenosis pairing: forward flow is forced through a narrowed opening. A leaking valve is blowing, with volume overload.

set1.q: Which finding distinguishes tricuspid regurgitation from mitral regurgitation?
opts: The murmur is holosystolic
Both tricuspid and mitral regurgitation are holosystolic, so timing cannot separate them. The inspiratory increase (Carvallo sign) does.
The murmur is blowing
Both regurgitant murmurs are blowing. The distinguishing feature of tricuspid regurgitation is the inspiratory increase, the Carvallo sign.
The murmur softens on standing
Standing softens mitral regurgitation too, so it does not discriminate. The Carvallo sign, louder on inspiration, marks tricuspid regurgitation.
It grows louder on inspiration

Correct. Both are holosystolic, but the tricuspid regurgitation murmur increases with inspiration, the Carvallo sign, because inspiration raises right-sided venous return. That distinguishes it from mitral regurgitation.

set1.q: Which medical measures treat severe, symptomatic tricuspid stenosis?
opts: Hydralazine, nitroprusside, intravenous fluids
Vasodilators suit aortic regurgitation, and extra fluid would worsen venous congestion. Tricuspid stenosis is treated with low salt, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist.
Warfarin, heparin bridging, antiplatelets
Warfarin with heparin bridging is the mechanical valve regimen. Tricuspid stenosis symptoms are treated with low salt, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist.
Low salt, diuretics, an aldosterone antagonist
Correct. Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, with bioprosthetic valve replacement preferred when surgery is needed.
Nitrates, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers
Nitrates, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are the classes avoided in aortic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is treated with low salt, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist.

set1.q: Where is the tricuspid regurgitation murmur heard?
opts: Right second space, radiating to the carotids
The second right intercostal space with radiation to the carotids is aortic stenosis. Tricuspid regurgitation is at the lower left sternal border.
Left second space, toward the right sternum
The left second intercostal space radiating toward the right sternal border is the pulmonic regurgitation murmur. Tricuspid regurgitation is lower, near the epigastrium.
Lower left sternal border, near the epigastrium
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur at the left mid or lower sternal border near the epigastrium that increases with inspiration (the Carvallo sign).
At the apex, radiating to the axilla
A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation sits at the lower left sternal border.

set1.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set1.q: How do mechanical and biological valves differ in anticoagulation?
opts: Neither needs anticoagulation
Mechanical valves need lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy. Only biological valves avoid long-term anticoagulation.
Mechanical needs it lifelong; biological does not
Correct. A mechanical valve (titanium and carbon) needs lifelong anticoagulation, while a biological valve (pig or cow tissue) does not need anticoagulation beyond the immediate postoperative period.
Biological needs it lifelong; mechanical does not
This is reversed. Mechanical valves need lifelong anticoagulation, while biological tissue valves do not beyond the immediate postoperative period.
Both need lifelong anticoagulation
Only the mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation. A biological valve needs none beyond the immediate postoperative period.

set1.q: How is the mitral stenosis murmur best heard?
opts: With the diaphragm, patient squatting
The diaphragm suits high-pitched sounds, and the mitral stenosis rumble is low-pitched. It is heard with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position.
With the bell, patient in left lateral decubitus
Correct. The low-pitched rumble of mitral stenosis is heard best with the bell at the apex, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position (lying on the left side).
With the diaphragm, patient sitting forward
Sitting forward brings the aortic valve closer to the chest wall and helps with aortic murmurs. The mitral rumble needs the bell with the patient on the left side.
With the bell, patient standing upright
Standing reduces venous return and would soften most murmurs. The mitral rumble is best with the bell in the left lateral decubitus position.

set2.q: Which valve lesion goes with a Corrigan pulse?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation gives a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. The collapsing Corrigan pulse is aortic regurgitation.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations and a venous thrill. The Corrigan arterial pulse belongs to aortic regurgitation.
Aortic regurgitation

Correct. A Corrigan pulse, the water hammer or collapsing pulse, has a very rapid upstroke followed by a rapid collapse. It goes with chronic aortic regurgitation, and a question may name it without describing it.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis gives the opposite pulse: a weak, delayed carotid upstroke, a clue to severe disease when felt with a forceful apex beat.

set2.q: Which regurgitant fraction marks severe mitral regurgitation?
opts: 20% or more
Twenty percent is mild mitral regurgitation, under 30%. Severe is a regurgitant fraction of 50% or more.
40% or more
Forty percent sits inside the moderate band of 30 to 49%. Severe mitral regurgitation starts at 50%.
50% or more
Correct. Severe mitral regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction of 50% or more, half of the stroke volume going back into the left atrium. Moderate is 30 to 49% and mild under 30%.
30% or more
A 30% threshold sweeps in moderate disease, 30 to 49%. Severe mitral regurgitation begins at a regurgitant fraction of 50%.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for valvular heart disease
set2.q: Which event produces the first heart sound (S1)?
opts: Aortic and pulmonic valves closing
Closure of the semilunar valves, aortic and pulmonic, produces the second heart sound at the end of systole, not the first.
Rapid filling of a dilated ventricle
Rapid filling of a dilated, volume-loaded left ventricle in early diastole produces the third heart sound, the systolic heart failure sound.
Atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle
Atrial contraction against a hypertrophied, pressure-loaded ventricle produces the fourth heart sound late in diastole, just before the first.
Mitral and tricuspid valves closing
Correct. The first heart sound is the atrioventricular valves, mitral and tricuspid, closing as the ventricles begin to contract. It marks the start of systole.

set2.q: Which transcatheter device repairs a leaking mitral valve without replacing it?
opts: Tricuspid annuloplasty ring
Annuloplasty repairs tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation. The transcatheter repair for mitral regurgitation is the mitral valve clip.
A mitral valve clip

Correct. A mitral valve clip grasps the leaflets to reduce the leak. The other surgical options for mitral regurgitation are transcatheter mitral valve replacement or a mechanical or biological valve.
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy opens a stenotic mitral valve; it would not stop a leak. The repair device for mitral regurgitation is the mitral valve clip.
Transcatheter aortic valve
A transcatheter aortic valve replaces the aortic valve in aortic stenosis. The mitral regurgitation repair device is the mitral valve clip.

set2.q: Which electrocardiogram findings fit pulmonic stenosis?
opts: Right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy

Correct. Pulmonic stenosis raises right ventricular pressure, and the electrocardiogram shows right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy. The echo shows abnormal valve motion and a raised jet on Doppler.
Left axis deviation, left ventricular hypertrophy
Left-sided hypertrophy belongs to aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic stenosis loads the right ventricle.
Left atrial abnormality, atrial fibrillation
Left atrial abnormality with atrial fibrillation is the mitral stenosis pattern. Pulmonic stenosis gives right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Right atrial enlargement, no ventricular change
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular change is tricuspid stenosis. Pulmonic stenosis thickens the right ventricle.

set2.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set2.q: Which drug is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist for a mechanical valve?
opts: Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and antiplatelets are ranked below vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves. The vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent, not a vitamin K antagonist. The most commonly used vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Warfarin

Correct. Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, the long-term anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves; if surgery requires heparin instead, warfarin is bridged until the ratio is therapeutic.
Heparin
Heparin is not a vitamin K antagonist; it is the bridging agent used around surgery. The most common vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.

set2.q: Which electrocardiogram finding points to tricuspid stenosis?
opts: Left ventricular hypertrophy out of proportion to the left atrium
Left ventricular hypertrophy is the aortic stenosis and chronic aortic regurgitation finding. Tricuspid stenosis shows right atrial enlargement.
Right atrial enlargement out of proportion to the right ventricle
Correct. Tricuspid stenosis shows right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy, because the obstruction sits behind the right atrium and spares the ventricle.
Left atrial enlargement out of proportion to the left ventricle
Left atrial abnormality with a spared left ventricle is the mitral stenosis pattern. Tricuspid stenosis enlarges the right atrium.
Right ventricular hypertrophy out of proportion to the right atrium
Dominant right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation fits pulmonic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis enlarges the right atrium more than the ventricle.

set2.q: Tricuspid stenosis obstructs flow between which chambers?
opts: Right atrium to right ventricle

Correct. Tricuspid stenosis narrows the valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, obstructing inflow; the right atrium dilates and hypertrophies, with low cardiac output and portal congestion.
Left atrium to left ventricle
Obstruction between the left atrium and left ventricle is mitral stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis blocks inflow from the right atrium to the right ventricle.
Right ventricle to pulmonary artery
Obstruction of right ventricular outflow to the lungs is pulmonic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis obstructs inflow from the right atrium.
Left ventricle to aorta
Obstruction of left ventricular outflow is aortic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis obstructs right atrial to right ventricular inflow.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for valvular heart disease
set2.q: Which ventricle does a fourth heart sound (S4) point to?
opts: A thin, dilated right ventricle
The fourth heart sound is framed around a hypertrophied, pressure-loaded left ventricle, not a thin dilated right one, which is a volume-overload picture.
A thick, hypertrophied left ventricle
Correct. The fourth heart sound is the high-pressure sound of diastolic heart failure: left ventricular hypertrophy, as from aortic stenosis, with the atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle.
A dilated, volume-loaded left ventricle
A dilated, volume-loaded ventricle gives the third heart sound, the sound of systolic heart failure and backflow such as aortic regurgitation.
A normal ventricle closing its valves
Valve closure produces the first and second heart sounds in any heart. The fourth heart sound signals a hypertrophied, stiff left ventricle.

set2.q: What is the management approach to pulmonic regurgitation?
opts: Tricuspid annuloplasty
Annuloplasty repairs tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating the underlying condition.
Treat the underlying condition
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating the underlying condition, with referral when it is seen on an echocardiogram or when right heart failure symptoms and signs appear.
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty opens a stenotic pulmonic valve, and outflow tract procedures like it are the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation, not its treatment.
Lifelong anticoagulation
Lifelong anticoagulation is for mechanical heart valves. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating the underlying condition.

set2.q: For tricuspid stenosis, what is balloon valvotomy reserved for?
opts: Every patient with a murmur
An audible murmur alone does not justify valvotomy. It is reserved for hepatic congestion that may progress to cirrhosis or severe venous congestion.
Mild disease without symptoms
Mild, asymptomatic disease is not an indication. Valvotomy is reserved for hepatic congestion threatening cirrhosis or severe venous congestion.
Children and young adults only
Age is the valvuloplasty rule for aortic stenosis. In tricuspid stenosis, valvotomy is reserved for hepatic or severe systemic venous congestion.
Hepatic congestion risking cirrhosis
Correct. Balloon valvotomy and valve repair are reserved for tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion that may lead to cirrhosis, or severe systemic venous congestion.

set2.q: What is the treatment for acute severe aortic regurgitation?
opts: Watchful waiting with repeat echo
Only the chronic form stays silent for 10 to 15 years. Acute severe aortic regurgitation causes cardiogenic shock and needs emergency surgery.
Emergency valve replacement or repair
Correct. Acute severe aortic regurgitation is treated with emergency aortic valve replacement or repair, ideally within 24 hours; the patient presents in cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema.
Afterload reduction with hydralazine
Afterload reduction is the medical management of chronic aortic regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction or no symptoms. The acute severe lesion needs emergency surgery.
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy opens a stenotic mitral valve. It has no place in acute aortic regurgitation, which needs emergency valve replacement or repair.

set2.q: Which change makes the pulmonic regurgitation murmur louder?
opts: Expiration
Expiration reduces venous return to the right heart and softens pulmonic regurgitation. Inspiration makes it louder.
Sitting upright
Moving from supine to upright reduces venous return. The pulmonic regurgitation murmur is louder lying supine, squatting or on inspiration.
Squatting
Correct. Anything that increases venous return makes the pulmonic regurgitation murmur louder: inspiration, squatting and lying supine. Expiration and standing, which reduce venous return, soften it.
Standing
Standing reduces venous return, so the pulmonic regurgitation murmur gets softer, not louder.

set2.q: Pulmonic stenosis is commonly part of which congenital condition?
opts: Ankylosing spondylitis
Ankylosing spondylitis is a valvular cause of aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic stenosis is commonly part of tetralogy of Fallot.
Tetralogy of Fallot
Correct. Pulmonic stenosis is commonly part of tetralogy of Fallot. It is almost always congenital, and carcinoid disease is the other listed cause.
Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome dilates the aortic root and causes aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic stenosis is commonly part of tetralogy of Fallot.
A bicuspid aortic valve
A bicuspid aortic valve is the leading cause of aortic stenosis under 70. Pulmonic stenosis is commonly part of tetralogy of Fallot.

set2.q: Why is rheumatic mitral stenosis rare in developed countries?
opts: Degenerative disease has replaced it
Degenerative, atherosclerotic disease is the leading cause of aortic stenosis over 70, not of mitral stenosis. Mitral stenosis is rare where rheumatic fever is rare.
Bicuspid valves are repaired at birth
A bicuspid valve is a congenital aortic problem and the leading cause of aortic stenosis under 70. It has nothing to do with the rarity of mitral stenosis.
Balloon valvotomy prevents narrowing
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy treats severe symptomatic mitral stenosis once it exists. The disease is rare because rheumatic fever has become uncommon.
Rheumatic fever has become less common
Correct. Mitral stenosis is rare in developed countries because the incidence of rheumatic fever, its most common cause, has fallen there.

set2.q: What treatment does uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse usually need?
opts: Usually none

Correct. Mitral valve prolapse usually needs no treatment. If it progresses to mitral regurgitation, the options are a clip, transcatheter mitral valve replacement, or a biological or mechanical valve.
Lifelong anticoagulation
Lifelong anticoagulation is for mechanical heart valves, not for a benign, asymptomatic prolapse.
Early valve replacement
Replacement is considered only if prolapse progresses to significant mitral regurgitation. Uncomplicated prolapse usually needs no treatment.
Balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy opens a stenotic mitral valve. A prolapsing, redundant valve usually needs no treatment at all.

set2.q: Which study should any patient with symptoms suggestive of aortic stenosis receive?
opts: A chest radiograph
A chest radiograph cannot show leaflet calcification or grade stenosis. Symptoms suggestive of aortic stenosis call for an echocardiogram.
An electrocardiogram alone
Left ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram has low sensitivity for aortic stenosis. Suggestive symptoms call for an echocardiogram.
An echocardiogram

Correct. Exertional chest pressure, shortness of breath or syncope suggestive of aortic stenosis calls for an echocardiogram, which shows thickened, calcified leaflets with reduced opening and grades severity.
A left heart catheterization
Catheterization is the definitive study, but it is not the first step for suggestive symptoms. Any patient with those symptoms should get an echocardiogram.

set2.q: What is the usual course of mitral valve prolapse?
opts: Rapidly fatal within years
Rapid mortality belongs to symptomatic aortic stenosis, 75% at 3 years. Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign and asymptomatic.
Relentlessly progressive stenosis
Prolapse does not narrow the valve. It is usually benign, and the complication to watch for is mitral regurgitation.
Heart failure by middle age
Heart failure is not the usual course. Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign and asymptomatic, occasionally progressing to mitral regurgitation.
Benign and asymptomatic
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign and asymptomatic, needing no treatment unless it progresses to mitral regurgitation.

set2.q: Which symptoms appear in severe tricuspid regurgitation?
opts: Angina and exertional syncope
Angina and exertional syncope are cardinal symptoms of aortic stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.
Head bobbing and wide pulses
Head bobbing and a wide pulse pressure are chronic aortic regurgitation signs. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.
Pedal edema and ascites
Correct. Mild to moderate tricuspid regurgitation is usually asymptomatic; severe disease causes pedal edema and ascites as systemic venous pressure rises.
Hemoptysis and hoarseness
Hemoptysis and hoarseness come from the high-pressure, enlarged left atrium of mitral stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.

set2.q: Primary tricuspid regurgitation from infective endocarditis is typical of whom?
opts: Intravenous drug users
Correct. Primary tricuspid regurgitation comes from infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users. Endocarditis from other sources more often involves the mitral valve.
Healthy women aged 15 to 30
Healthy women 15 to 30 are the typical patients with mitral valve prolapse. Tricuspid endocarditis is typical of intravenous drug users.
Adults older than 70
Over 70 the leading valve problem is degenerative aortic stenosis. Primary tricuspid regurgitation from endocarditis is typical of intravenous drug users.
Children with tetralogy of Fallot
Tetralogy of Fallot commonly includes pulmonic stenosis. Tricuspid endocarditis is typical of intravenous drug users.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for valvular heart disease
set2.q: Which valve lies beneath the second intercostal space at the left sternal border?
opts: Aortic
The aortic area is the mirror image: the second intercostal space at the right sternal border. The left side at that level is the pulmonic area.
Tricuspid
The tricuspid area is the fifth intercostal space at the lower left sternal border. The second intercostal space on the left is the pulmonic area.
Mitral
The mitral area is the apex, at the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. The second intercostal space at the left sternal border is the pulmonic area.
Pulmonic

Correct. The pulmonic area is the second intercostal space at the left sternal border. Questions give the location in these anatomic terms rather than naming the area, so the valve underneath has to be known.

set2.q: Which advice fits a patient with aortic stenosis?
opts: Start high-intensity interval training
Strenuous physical activity and competitive sports are to be avoided in aortic stenosis, because exertion can provoke angina, syncope and heart failure.
Carry a nitrate for exertional chest pain
Nitrates are avoided in aortic stenosis with angina because they drop preload. The advice is to avoid strenuous activity and dehydration.
Avoid strenuous activity and competitive sports
Correct. Medical care for mild and moderate aortic stenosis rests on the preload-dependent physiology: avoid strenuous physical activity and competitive sports, and avoid dehydration and hypovolemia.
Restrict fluids to lower cardiac workload
Fluid restriction risks hypovolemia, which is exactly what a preload-dependent patient with aortic stenosis must avoid. The advice is to avoid strenuous exertion and dehydration.

set2.q: What is the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation?
opts: Iatrogenic injury

Correct. The most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation is iatrogenic: surgical valvotomy, valvectomy or valvuloplasty done to relieve right ventricular outflow tract obstruction leaves the valve leaking.
Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension is the high-pressure cause of pulmonic regurgitation, but it is not the most common. Iatrogenic injury after outflow tract procedures is.
Carcinoid disease
Carcinoid disease is a low-pressure cause of pulmonic regurgitation, but not the most common one. Iatrogenic injury is.
A bicuspid valve
A congenital bicuspid pulmonic valve is a low-pressure cause, but the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation is iatrogenic.

set2.q: In mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation is a risk factor for what?
opts: Papillary muscle rupture
Papillary muscle rupture follows acute myocardial infarction and causes acute mitral regurgitation. Atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis raises thromboembolic risk.
Thromboembolism
Correct. Left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation, and atrial fibrillation is a risk factor for thromboembolism, one of the main dangers of mitral stenosis.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is a root cause of acute aortic regurgitation. In mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation raises the risk of thromboembolism.
Rheumatic fever recurrence
Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune reaction to group A streptococci, not a consequence of the rhythm. Atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis raises thromboembolic risk.

set2.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set2.q: What is the target international normalized ratio for a mechanical aortic valve?
opts: Correct. A mechanical aortic valve targets an international normalized ratio of 2.5, range 2.0 to 3.0. A mechanical mitral valve, or valves in both positions, targets 3.0.
A target of 3.0, range 2.5 to 3.5, is for a mechanical mitral valve or for valves in both positions. The aortic target is 2.5.
A ratio of 1.5 is below any mechanical valve target. The mechanical aortic valve target is 2.5, range 2.0 to 3.0.
A ratio of 4.0 exceeds every mechanical valve target. The aortic target is 2.5, and the highest target, mitral or both, is 3.0.

set2.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
set2.q: Which is avoided as the sole long-term therapy for a mechanical heart valve?
opts: A vitamin K antagonist
A vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin is exactly the recommended long-term therapy for mechanical valves. Antiplatelet therapy alone is what falls short.
Warfarin
Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist and the recommended therapy for mechanical valves, not something to avoid.
Warfarin with a heparin bridge for surgery
Bridging warfarin with heparin around surgery is required, not avoided. Antiplatelet therapy alone is inadequate for a mechanical valve.
An antiplatelet agent
Correct. Vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for the long-term management of mechanical valves, so an antiplatelet agent alone is not adequate.

set2.q: Who accounts for most mitral stenosis caused by rheumatic fever?
opts: Men, about 80%
Eighty percent male describes symptomatic aortic stenosis. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is the reverse, about 80% women.
Children under 10
Rheumatic mitral stenosis takes about 20 years to be diagnosed after the fever, so it is not a disease of young children. About 80% of patients are women.
Adults older than 70
Age over 70 is the setting of degenerative aortic stenosis. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is defined by sex, about 80% women, and by the 20-year lag after rheumatic fever.
Women, about 80%
Correct. About 80% of mitral stenosis due to rheumatic fever occurs in women. By contrast, 80% of patients with symptomatic aortic stenosis are men.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for valvular heart disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
set2.q: Who is the typical patient with mitral valve prolapse?
opts: A healthy woman aged 15 to 30
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is usually found in healthy women 15 to 30 years old, is usually benign and asymptomatic, and is heard as a mid-systolic click at the apex.
A man older than 70
Older men with a harsh systolic murmur suggest degenerative aortic stenosis. Mitral valve prolapse is typical of healthy young women.
A person who injects drugs
Injection drug use points to tricuspid valve endocarditis and primary tricuspid regurgitation. Mitral valve prolapse is typical of healthy women 15 to 30.
A child with tetralogy of Fallot
Tetralogy of Fallot commonly includes pulmonic stenosis. Mitral valve prolapse is typical of healthy women 15 to 30.

set2.q: Which drug relieves dyspnea and orthopnea in mitral stenosis?
opts: A loop diuretic
Correct. Symptoms of dyspnea and orthopnea in mitral stenosis are treated with loop diuretics such as furosemide or bumetanide, which relieve the pulmonary congestion.
A nitrate
Nitrates are named in the aortic stenosis avoid list. The medical treatment for mitral stenosis symptoms is a loop diuretic.
Hydralazine
Hydralazine is an afterload-reducing agent for chronic aortic regurgitation. Mitral stenosis dyspnea and orthopnea are treated with loop diuretics.
Warfarin
Warfarin is the vitamin K antagonist for mechanical heart valves. Loop diuretics treat the congestive symptoms of mitral stenosis.

set2.q: Which procedure treats tricuspid regurgitation caused by annular dilation?
opts: A mitral valve clip
A mitral valve clip treats mitral regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation is treated with annuloplasty.
Annuloplasty
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation is treated with annuloplasty after treating the underlying condition; valve repair or replacement is used when the cause is primary.
Valve replacement
Replacement, like repair, is used when tricuspid regurgitation has a primary cause such as endocarditis. Annular dilation is treated with annuloplasty.
Balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy opens a stenotic valve; it would worsen a leak. Annular dilation is treated with annuloplasty.
